title: How the funds vote
gist: Vanguard describes a deliberately decentralized proxy-voting architecture: roughly two dozen internal and external managers vote across 400+ funds, and as of 2026 U.S. internally managed fund voting was split from one stewardship group into two separate teams (VCMIS and VPMIS). The stated posture is explicit deference to boards and management — the passive U.S. funds will not submit shareholder proposals or nominate directors — while the Investor Choice program pushes voting power down to end investors in a growing number of funds. The page is primarily a disclosure/navigation hub, so the signal is structural rather than analytical.

insights.claim: Vanguard's proxy votes are not cast by a single centralized body: across more than 400 funds worldwide, roughly two dozen internal and external investment managers vote on behalf of the funds or fund portions they manage.
insights.speaker: Vanguard Research
insights.so_what: Treating 'Vanguard' as one monolithic voting bloc misreads the ownership map; campaigns and vote-outcome models need to account for up to two dozen separate decision-makers with different policies.
insights.quote: Across Vanguard’s more than 400 funds worldwide, some two dozen internal and external investment managers cast proxy votes on behalf of the respective funds—or portion of funds—that they manage.

insights.claim: Proxy voting for Vanguard's internally managed U.S. funds is administered by two separate and distinct teams — Vanguard Capital Management Investment Stewardship (VCMIS) and Vanguard Portfolio Management Investment Stewardship (VPMIS) — each with its own approach and voting policies.
insights.speaker: Vanguard Research
insights.so_what: Two policy sets inside the same asset manager can produce split votes on the same ballot item; watch for divergence between VCMIS- and VPMIS-stewarded fund lists on contested governance votes.
insights.quote: Two separate and distinct teams administer proxy voting on behalf of Vanguard’s internally managed U.S. funds
insights.locator: Proxy voting on behalf of Vanguard’s internally managed U.S. funds

insights.claim: The VCMIS/VPMIS split is new as of 2026 — prior to that year, voting for Vanguard's internally advised funds was administered by a single group, Vanguard Investment Stewardship.
insights.speaker: Vanguard Research
insights.so_what: Historical Vanguard voting records are not apples-to-apples with post-2026 data; any time series on index-manager voting behavior needs a structural break at 2026.
insights.quote: Prior to the establishment of VCMIS and VPMIS in 2026, proxy voting on behalf of Vanguard’s internally advised funds was administered by Vanguard Investment Stewardship.

insights.claim: Where a fund is managed by multiple advisors, each external advisor's vote is disclosed separately in the vote record rather than aggregated to a single fund-level position.
insights.speaker: Vanguard Research
insights.so_what: Vote-record scraping must dedupe at the advisor level; a single fund can show internally conflicting votes on the same resolution.
insights.quote: If a fund is managed by multiple advisors, each external advisor’s vote will display in the record.

insights.claim: The passively managed U.S. index equity funds and ETFs explicitly do not seek to dictate company strategy or operations, do not submit shareholder proposals, and do not nominate board members.
insights.speaker: Vanguard Research
insights.so_what: Activists and issuers should not expect the largest passive holder to originate campaigns; pressure has to come from active holders, with Vanguard votes as a swing factor rather than an instigator.
insights.quote: these passive U.S. funds do not seek to dictate company strategy or operations, submit shareholder proposals, or nominate board members
insights.locator: Proxy voting on behalf of Vanguard’s internally managed U.S. funds

insights.claim: The stated governance principle is that precise strategies and tactics for maximizing long-term investment returns belong to a company's board of directors and management team, not to the index fund shareholder.
insights.speaker: Vanguard Research
insights.so_what: This is a deliberate step back from the 'universal owner as steward' consensus that drove index-manager engagement in the prior decade — it lowers the odds of passive-money support for prescriptive ESG or strategy resolutions.
insights.quote: The precise strategies and tactics for maximizing long-term investment returns should be decided by a company’s board of directors and management team.

insights.claim: Voting is framed as being conducted under stated voting policies in pursuit of each fund's stated investment objective, rather than under a firmwide house view on governance or corporate behavior.
insights.speaker: Vanguard Research
insights.so_what: Grounding votes in per-fund investment objectives narrows the legal and political attack surface on index managers and makes fiduciary-duty challenges to their voting harder to sustain.
insights.quote: The managers administer proxy voting in accordance with the stated voting policies and in pursuit of each fund’s stated investment objective.

insights.claim: Investor Choice, which gives end investors a greater voice in how their equity index funds vote, has moved past its pilot stage and is offered in a growing number of Vanguard funds.
insights.speaker: Vanguard Research
insights.so_what: Pass-through voting mechanically dilutes the concentrated voting power of the big index complexes; as coverage grows, forecasting outcomes at large-cap meetings gets noisier and campaign targeting gets harder.
insights.quote: A growing number of Vanguard funds offer investors in those funds a greater voice in the proxy voting process through Investor Choice.

insights.claim: Investors in the Investor Choice pilot directed how their equity index funds voted at select company shareholder meetings, and those directed votes are separately disclosed in a dedicated Investor Choice report.
insights.speaker: Vanguard Research
insights.so_what: The Investor Choice record is a rare dataset on what retail index holders actually want on governance ballots — useful for anticipating where pass-through voting shifts outcomes versus the manager default.

insights.claim: Vanguard publishes Investor Choice Voting Briefs explaining how its U.S. equity index funds voted on important governance topics, including how the voting policy options offered through Investor Choice were applied.
insights.speaker: Vanguard Research
insights.so_what: The briefs are a low-latency read on stewardship reasoning at specific meetings — a cheaper leading indicator than waiting for the annual N-PX dump.

themes.theme: Disclosure cadence and operational risk points

insights.claim: U.S. fund votes are disclosed annually on Form N-PX to the SEC under the Investment Company Act of 1940 for the proxy year ended June 30, 2026, while global fund disclosure covers the prior two proxy years and the current proxy year is published quarterly on a rolling basis.
insights.speaker: Vanguard Research
insights.so_what: The quarterly rolling global feed is materially fresher than the annual N-PX filing — the faster channel to monitor if you track index-manager voting shifts in near real time.

insights.claim: Both stewardship teams operate under named operational policies covering third-party service provider oversight, securities lending and proxy voting, and proxy voting conflicts of interest.
insights.speaker: Vanguard Research
insights.so_what: Securities lending and proxy-advisor reliance are where voting power actually leaks or gets outsourced — these three policies are the pressure points for anyone assessing how much of a share's vote is truly cast.
insights.locator: Information about operational procedures and policies

insights.claim: The internally managed U.S. funds predominantly track benchmarks set by independent index providers, which is presented as the reason those funds refrain from directing company strategy.
insights.speaker: Vanguard Research
insights.so_what: It reinforces that real allocation power sits with the index providers who define the benchmarks, not with the manager casting the votes.
insights.quote: passively managed index equity funds and ETFs that seek to track benchmarks determined by independent index providers
insights.locator: Proxy voting on behalf of Vanguard’s internally managed U.S. funds
